legal.hook: Can PMLA adjudicating authority function without judicial member?

The bench has not yet issued its judgment, meaning the legal position remains unsettled. The case turns on whether the composition requirement under the PMLA—which mandates both a judicial and technical member—is so fundamental that proceedings cannot lawfully continue with only one member present. This has direct operational consequences for the Enforcement Directorate's PMLA prosecution workflow, as adjudicating authorities across the country currently handle confiscation and attachment orders. The Court's decision will clarify whether past orders passed without a full bench are valid, and whether pending cases can proceed with reduced composition.
legal.contextNote: The issue engages Section 4 of the PMLA, 2002, which prescribes the constitution of the Adjudicating Authority (one judicial member, one technical member). legal.headline: Custody of minor daughter with her grandparent not wrongful confinement under Mohammedan Law: Gujarat HC
legal.hook: The Court held that Mohammedan Law's recognition of the mother's custodial right up to puberty does not automatically render the custody of the minor with her grandparent wrongful
legal.summary: The Gujarat High Court ruled that custody of a minor daughter by her grandparent does not constitute wrongful confinement under Mohammedan Law, even though Islamic law recognizes the mother's custodial right until the child reaches puberty. The court clarified that the statutory recognition of maternal custody rights does not automatically render alternative custody arrangements—such as with a grandparent—unlawful or constitute criminal wrongful confinement. The judgment addresses a factual dispute over guardianship and custody rather than a straightforward violation of established maternal rights. The court's holding suggests that courts retain discretion to recognize de facto or legally sanctioned guardianship arrangements outside the default custodial framework, particularly when the minor's welfare and family circumstances warrant it. The decision signals that Mohammedan Law's custodial rules operate as presumptions rather than absolute bars to other arrangements.
legal.contextNote: This applies to Section 494 (wrongful confinement) read with Muslim Personal Law (Shariat) Application Act, 1937, Section 2, and the Guardianship and Wards Act, 1890. The court's reasoning hinges on distinguishing between statutory custodial *preference* and criminal *confinement*—a meaningful distinction absent from earlier Gujarat case law on point. The practical implication: (1) family law practitioners must recognize that maternal custody under Islamic law, while presumptively favored, is not enforceable as an absolute criminal prohibition on other guardians holding the child lawfully; (2) in-house counsel handling custody disputes involving Muslim parties should anticipate arguments that non-maternal custody may be permissible if the minor's interests align, requiring fact-intensive welfare analysis rather than formulaic application of the personal law rule; (3) criminal sections cannot be weaponized to override civil guardianship determinations absent actual unlawful restraint or deprivation of liberty.

The move reinforces the government's push toward RuPay adoption as a domestic alternative to Visa and Mastercard while protecting consumer access to zero-cost digital payments in the sub-₹2,000 segment, which covers a majority of daily retail transactions in India.
legal.contextNote: Section 10A of the PSS Act, 2007 grants the Finance Ministry (via the Reserve Bank) broad authority to regulate payment system charges and impose conditions on system participants to achieve public interest objectives. (1) Fintech platforms and payment aggregators must audit their merchant onboarding agreements and settlement systems to ensure no hidden or indirect fees (e.g., markup on MDR, convenience surcharges, or settlement delays) are imposed on RuPay/UPI transactions ≤₹2,000; breach exposes operators to RBI enforcement action under PSS Act Section 27. legal.headline: POSH limitation runs from the last incident, not the fear or apprehension in the mind of the complainant: Calcutta HC
legal.hook: Law of limitation may harshly affect a particular party, but it has to be applied with all its rigour when the statute so prescribes
legal.summary: The Calcutta High Court has ruled that the limitation period for filing complaints under the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013 (POSH Act) runs from the date of the last incident of harassment, not from when the complainant first felt fear or apprehension. The court emphasised that while limitation law may operate harshly in individual cases, courts must apply it with full rigour when the statute mandates it. The judgment clarifies that subjective emotional distress or psychological unease does not extend the limitation clock—only the actual occurrence of a fresh act of harassment restarts or extends the period. The ruling rejected a complainant's argument that the limitation should commence from when she developed apprehension about future harassment rather than from concrete incidents.
legal.contextNote: This applies Section 27 (read with Section 19) of the POSH Act, 2013, which prescribes a three-year limitation for complaints, measured objectively. The Calcutta HC has aligned with a strict chronological reading: limitation attaches to *events*, not mental states. For in-house counsel: (1) Document the precise date of each alleged incident; vague references to 'ongoing hostility' or 'persistent dread' without timestamped conduct will not extend the window; (2) Advise complainants and HR teams that delay in reporting after the last concrete act of harassment is fatal—three years from that act, not from when someone 'should have' felt brave enough to complain; (3) In IC handling POSH complaints, scrutinise whether each alleged act falls within the limitation period independently; a single stale incident buried in a mixed timeline will be barred even if other recent acts are live.
